office.title: Indiana School Board Member
office.summary: A school board is the elected or appointed governing body of a public school corporation, the legal unit that runs a local school district [1, 2]. The board hires and evaluates the superintendent, adopts policies, and approves the annual budget, while the superintendent and staff run schools day to day [3]. Most boards have five or seven members serving staggered four-year terms [3]. Starting in 2026, candidates may list a political party, run as independents, or list no affiliation on the ballot, and there is no primary for these seats [2, 4].

facts.label: Term
facts.value: 4 years, with elections staggered so part of the board is chosen every two years [3]

facts.label: Elected
facts.value: At the November general election (November 3, 2026, or November 2028 for some seats); depending on the local organization plan, members represent the whole school corporation (at large) or a district within it, and some boards are wholly or partly appointed [2]

facts.label: Ballot label
facts.value: Each candidate chooses a party label, 'Independent', or no affiliation, shown next to the name; no primary and no straight-ticket voting for these races [2, 4]

facts.label: Pay
facts.value: Set by board resolution: an annual amount of no more than 10% of the lowest starting teacher salary in the school corporation, plus a capped per diem [5]

duties: Hires, evaluates and can dismiss the superintendent, and approves the hiring and firing of principals, teachers and other staff recommended by the superintendent [1, 7, 3].
Adopts the annual budget, appropriates funds and oversees school finances [1, 3].

Decides whether to ask voters to approve an operating referendum (an extra property tax levy); the board adopts the resolution and the Department of Local Government Finance reviews the ballot language for compliance with state law [8].
Approves contracts, buys and sells property, and decides on construction, repair and demolition of school buildings [1].

Bargains with the teachers' union over salary, wages and wage-related benefits such as health insurance and retirement; state law excludes teacher evaluation procedures from those bargaining subjects [9].
Writes and updates policies and rules for schools, often in a policy handbook, including the student handbook [1, 3].
Buys curricular materials, provides them to students without charge, and runs programs such as student transportation and school lunch [1].

Must adopt a process for parents and residents to ask that library material be removed as obscene or harmful to minors, review requests at public meetings and keep a public catalog of library materials [10].
Hears written appeals of student expulsions, unless the board has voted not to hear them [11].
Must take official action openly; Indiana's Open Door Law says public agencies' official action is to be conducted openly so the people may be fully informed [12, 13].

A school board member must have lived in the school corporation (and, for a district seat, the district) for at least one year before the election, and a teacher or other employee of the school corporation may not serve on its board [2].

What the board does not control: the State Board of Education adopts statewide academic standards [14], the General Assembly sets the state school funding formula in the state budget [15], and voucher (Choice Scholarship) eligibility is set by state law [16].
recent_changes: 2025: Senate Enrolled Act 287 allowed school board candidates to declare a party affiliation; the Indiana School Boards Association opposed the change, and a supporter quoted by WNDU, a Noblesville school board member, said it adds transparency [17].

2026: Candidates choose a party, 'Independent' or no affiliation on their nominating petition, and that choice appears on the ballot; a candidate claiming the Democratic or Republican party must have voted in that party's primary in the two most recent primaries they voted in, or have certification from the county party chair, or can be challenged and removed from the ballot [2].

July 2026: Chalkbeat reported, citing Indiana School Boards Association data, that 524 of 1,044 candidates chose a party, about 72% of them Republicans [18]; the Indiana Election Division's 2026 guidance and the wording of the law differ on the primary-voting test, a question county election boards decide [19].

February 2026: Senate Enrolled Act 25 set the order of school board candidates on the ballot, grouped by party, with candidates who list no affiliation placed after the party and independent candidates [20].

2025: Senate Enrolled Act 1, a property tax law, limits how much operating revenue districts can raise through taxes and restricts school referendums to statewide general elections in even-numbered years [21, 22].
2025: The same law requires districts to share operating revenue with brick-and-mortar charter schools that enroll their students, statewide starting in 2028 [21, 22].
2025: The state budget opened Choice Scholarship vouchers to all Indiana families starting in June 2026 [16].
2026: The Indianapolis Public Education Corporation, rather than the Indianapolis Public Schools board, now certifies Indianapolis Public Schools referendum questions for the ballot [20].

2023: Senate Enrolled Act 391 changed the so-called $1 law so the Indiana Department of Education can order districts that lost at least 10% of enrollment over five years to close schools under 60% capacity and offer them to charter schools [23].
2023: House Enrolled Act 1447 required school districts to set up procedures for complaints that library material is obscene or harmful to minors [10].

race_context: The Evansville Vanderburgh School Corporation (EVSC) serves Evansville and Vanderburgh County; WNIN describes it as serving more than 21,000 students and as Indiana's third-largest district [24]. The district lists 22 elementary, 8 middle and 7 high schools plus district-wide programs [25].

The board has seven members, elected by voters across Evansville and Vanderburgh County [24]. Seats are designated by district (District 1, District 2, etc.) or at large, and WNIN reports that voters across the county vote in the District 2 race [26].

Board president Mike Duckworth said the board hired superintendent Darla Hoover, who started in July 2025 [27]. In January 2026 the board chose Duckworth as president, Melissa Moore as vice president and Amy DeVries as secretary [24].

Four seats are on the 2026 ballot, with 10 candidates on the ballot after the June 18 filing deadline [28]. The state list shows District 2 as 'vote for 1', but WNIN reports that two District 2 seats are up and that voters will choose two of the four District 2 candidates [28, 26].

District 1: incumbent Chris Kiefer is unopposed [28]. District 2: incumbents Mike Duckworth and David Hollingsworth are running for reelection against Lindsey Patterson and Ken Colbert [26]. At Large: incumbent Melissa Moore faces Steve Ary, Andy Guarino, Brian Murphy and Alan Goad [29].

Partisan labels: Steve Ary is the only candidate listed with a party (Republican) and WNIN describes him as the first partisan EVSC board candidate under a new state law; the other nine filed as nonpartisan [28, 29]. A second Republican filer, Ryan Owens, withdrew during the grace period [28].

Safety audit (December 2025): on Dec. 15, 2025 the board approved a $215,000 district-wide security assessment of all 40 EVSC buildings, policies and crisis procedures by National School Safety and Security Services, the first district-wide study since 2008 [30].
Property-tax law (2025–2026): WNIN reported that EVSC 'will lose millions of dollars' under the 2025 property-tax law (SEA 1) [29]. This guide did not find an EVSC budget document stating the amount.
Student devices (2025–2026): candidates discussed the state-required limits on cell phones and other devices in schools [29, 26].

Forums and interviews: WNIN published interviews with the at-large candidates (Sept. 23), the District 2 incumbents (Oct. 1) and the District 2 challengers (Oct. 2) [29, 27, 26]. This guide did not find a 2026 candidate forum or newspaper questionnaire for this race.

Key differences: at-large challengers differ on priorities, from safety and device limits (Ary, Goad) to career education and employee health benefits (Murphy) and enrollment and teacher pay (Guarino) [29]. In District 2 the incumbents point to their records, while Colbert criticizes the board on transparency and Patterson says she would first learn how the board works [27, 26].

background: BallotReady lists him as faculty program chair for criminal justice at Ivy Tech Community College [31].
BallotReady lists his current District 1 term as running through Dec. 31, 2026, and shows him as a candidate for the same seat in 2022 [31].
path_to_ballot: Filed as a nonpartisan candidate and has no opponent on the ballot [28, 6].

items: Speaking about the district-wide security study in December 2025, he said its aim is to prevent incidents and that a comprehensive study helps the district respond quickly if a serious situation occurs [30].

gaps: No 2026 interview, questionnaire or campaign website found; WNIN's candidate coverage did not profile the uncontested District 1 race.
Seen only in search snippets (unverified): a Courier & Press report that the withdrawn Republican filer was running for District 1.
No campaign finance reports found.

candidates.summary: Incumbent District 2 trustee seeking a third term [27].
background: Retired ironworker who also drives a school bus part-time for EVSC [27].
PTA area council president and former vice president; he says he has received PTA awards, including a lifetime achievement award [27].
Has served two terms (eight years) on the board [26].

items: Says safety is his first priority [27].
Wants reading scores to rise; says the district has met some goals but must improve [27].
Says he wants to keep politics out of schools and does not want to be labeled as one party's member [27].

on_incumbent: Says the board has 'achieved some of our goals' but 'we need to get better,' and that his record 'speaks for itself' [27].
plans: Says he would continue his PTA work and use the board seat to talk with students, staff and bus drivers in district buildings [27].
gaps: WNIN's interview did not cover his views on the budget, the 2025 property-tax law, staffing or the device policy.
No campaign website, endorsements or campaign finance reports found.

candidates.summary: Challenger for one of the two District 2 seats; a local business owner who has criticized the board on transparency [26].
background: Owns a consignment shop in Evansville and co-founded the Indiana Freedom Caucus, according to WNIN [26].
Co-hosts the podcast 'Republicans in Bad Standing' [26].

items: WNIN reported that he criticizes the board for lacking transparency and says his public-records requests have gone unanswered for years [26].

In posts signed with his name on the Telegram channel 'ColbertReport', he says he backs 'Complete Transparency and a #studentfirst agenda' and says the current administration is not transparent about federal funding [32].
In a post on the same channel, he linked falling ACT scores to the board's past curriculum votes [32].

on_incumbent: WNIN reported he argued that incumbents benefit from name recognition [26].
His channel's posts urge voters to replace current board members whom he calls 'career politicians' [32].
gaps: Did not respond to WNIN's interview requests, per WNIN; positions here come from WNIN's summary and his own Telegram posts, which carry no calendar dates.

WNIN's article also reports that he and his podcast co-host were removed from the state and county Republican Party and that he faces a recent bench warrant related to an attempt to file as a Republican in another race; this guide could not confirm the details from court or party records.
No campaign website, endorsements or campaign finance reports found.

candidates.summary: First-time candidate and EVSC graduate challenging for one of the two District 2 seats [26].
background: Born and raised in Evansville; attended Delaware, Evans and North schools [26].
Parent of students in the district, including a North High School senior [26].

items: Called the district's security study a good idea [26].
On the state-required device policy, said the district's 'hands are probably tied a little bit' because it is state law [26].
Says she is running nonpartisan because 'politics needs to stay out of public education' [26].

on_incumbent: Told WNIN she needs more information before forming opinions on specific board policies [26].
plans: Her first priority would be learning how the board works and getting to know the superintendent and community [26].
gaps: No stated positions found on the budget, the 2025 property-tax law, staffing or academics.
No campaign website, endorsements or campaign finance reports found.

candidates.summary: Incumbent District 2 trustee and board president, with 26 non-consecutive years on the board [24, 27].
background: Retired from the sheriff's department in 1997, later worked as a local representative for U.S. Senators Richard Lugar and Dan Coats, and held city posts including water superintendent [27].
Was a Little League commissioner for 35 years [27].
Chosen board president in January 2026, his sixth time in the role [24].

items: Describes the district's budget as 'about a third of a billion dollar budget' and says careful use of taxpayer money is important [27].
Calls safety a 'main priority' and says the district works with city and county police [27].
Says the district is studying its facilities so it can spend money appropriately, and cites the Bosse High School overpass and athletic upgrades as accomplishments [27].
Wants to study redistricting and bus routes, saying early-morning and late-afternoon rides in the dark are 'dangerous' [27].
Points to the district's focus on students reading by third grade [27].
Says he has always run nonpartisan and that politics should be kept separate from the board; says vacancies should be filled by the board rather than party committees [27].

on_incumbent: Says the board's main job is hiring the superintendent and setting policy, and that he does not micromanage [27].
plans: Wants to review technology policies in light of state cell-phone rules [27].
gaps: No stated position found on the 2025 property-tax law (SEA 1) or a referendum.
No campaign website, endorsements or campaign finance reports found.

candidates.summary: Military veteran and maintenance supervisor challenging the at-large incumbent [29].
background: Served 14 years in the military; works as a maintenance tech supervisor for a property management company [29].

items: Says 'District security studies I'm all for and agree with' and raised concerns about safety in special-needs classrooms [29].
Wants better pay and support for teachers, who he says 'aren't being taken care of good enough' [29].
Supports the cell phone and gaming device ban, with medical exceptions [29].

on_incumbent: Says families feel unheard and that some trustees 'weren't paying attention' [29].
gaps: Answered WNIN's questions by email; no recorded interview, campaign website or other coverage found.
No stated positions found on the budget or the 2025 property-tax law.
No endorsements or campaign finance reports found.

candidates.summary: Former EVSC trustee and retired principal seeking to return to the board [29].
background: Was a principal for 17 years and an assistant principal for 10; holds master's degrees in adult education and special education [29].
Served on the EVSC board for about nine years, leaving four years ago; has served on the EVSC Foundation board and as president of Evansville Retired Teachers [29].
Has worked as a substitute in EVSC for more than 115 days over the past four years [29].

items: Lists the cell phone policy as his first priority [29].
Wants to 'make sure we don't lose any kids' amid competition from vouchers and charter schools [29].
Points to past board action removing a $60,000 salary cap, which he calls 'the biggest pay raise EVSC had ever given teachers at one time' [29].
Supports the outside security review, saying 'I thought it was a good study' [29].

on_incumbent: Calls incumbent Melissa Moore 'a very good person' and says he is running to return to the board, not against her [29].
gaps: WNIN's article gives his past tenure both as two terms plus a partial year and as 'nine years' without reconciling them.
No stated positions found on the budget or the 2025 property-tax law.
No campaign website, endorsements or campaign finance reports found.

candidates.summary: Home builder and Marine Corps veteran focused on career education and employee benefits [29].
background: Has lived in Evansville since 2000; served in the U.S. Marine Corps; runs a family home-building business and has done real estate development [29].
Taught career trades in the Dallas area and works on EVSC construction projects [29].

items: Says the 2025 property-tax law (SEA 1) will 'severely limit and restrict' school funding and expects referendums to be the likely response [29].
Wants to expand career education and the Southwest Indiana Career and Technical Center [29].
Criticizes IREAD and ILEARN testing for pushing teachers to 'teach to a test' [29].
Wants equal health-care options for all EVSC employees, including custodians and paraprofessionals [29].
Supports the comprehensive safety study [29].
Supports no screens in classrooms and would extend limits to Chromebooks [29].

on_incumbent: Says he offers 'a fresh perspective' and that board members may not fully understand construction projects [29].
plans: Wants the board to listen more to students [29].
gaps: No campaign website, endorsements or campaign finance reports found.

candidates.summary: Incumbent at-large trustee and board vice president, first elected in 2022 [24].
background: Navy veteran and life coach; Evansville native and Bosse High School graduate [29].
Elected to the board in 2022; board vice president since January 2026 [24].

items: Lists student success and literacy as priorities, citing 'increasing of literacy scores' [29].
Says she objected by email to a short graduation ceremony at one school and that this year's ceremonies were longer and more inclusive [29].

on_incumbent: Says she is running again 'because the work is not done' and that new members need time to get acclimated to the role [29].
endorsements_finance: WNIN reported that the county Republican Party has criticized county Democrats for supporting her [29].
gaps: WNIN's interview did not cover her views on the budget, the 2025 property-tax law, safety or staffing.
No campaign website or campaign finance reports found.

candidates.summary: Republican challenger for the at-large seat; WNIN calls him the first partisan EVSC board candidate [28].
background: Says he is a foster parent whose children attend EVSC schools [29].
Says he previously ran for county party chairman [29].
path_to_ballot: Filed as a Republican under a new state law allowing party labels in school board races [28, 6].
Explaining the label, he said, 'I believe it's important for people to know where you stand' [29].

items: Lists safety as his top priority and wants policy based on the district's safety audit; supports weapons detection systems while saying 'It's not a solution to everything' [29].
Says he is '100-percent for the banning of those devices' [29].
Wants 'social issues' kept out of classrooms [29].
Says foster children often arrive unable to read and 'We have to do better' [29].

on_incumbent: Criticizes the status quo, saying 'if you always do what you've always done, you'll always get what you've always got' [29].
plans: Wants to help foster children and students facing bullying, academic struggles and safety issues [29].
endorsements_finance: County Republican Chair Kyhle Moers said the party plans to support his campaign with door knocking, phone banking and mail [28].
gaps: How the party label was obtained (petition or party certification) was not described in sources found.
No stated positions found on the budget or the 2025 property-tax law.
No campaign website or campaign finance reports found.
